wv_county_line_boulders.blurb: A boulder-hunting spot inside Coopers Rock State Forest, a short drive east of Morgantown. The blocks here are small to medium sandstone boulders scattered in the woods, and most of the problems are on the friendlier side: plenty of easy lines and V1s, then a thinner tail of harder problems that reaches into the V7 and V8 range. It suits a mixed group, with warm-ups for newer climbers and a few tough projects for the strong. Bring pads, since landings vary, and give the rock time to dry after rain. Brush off holds and keep your shoes wiped between goes.
wv_county_line_boulders.parking_note: Enter the forest at the main gate and keep going toward the main overlook. Take the first pull-off on your right, the one with picnic tables and a trail sign.
wv_county_line_boulders.approach: From the picnic tables, head straight downhill into the trees, cross the roadside trail, and follow the rocky path a short way to the first small boulders.

wv_county_line_boulders_climbs.blurb: The bouldering at the County Line group in Coopers Rock State Forest, near Morgantown. These are sandstone boulders in the woods just off the main park road, with a gentle bias: lots of easy problems and V1s, a good handful in the V2 to V4 range, and only a few hard ones for people who want a project. Good for a relaxed session with a mixed crowd. Landings can be uneven, so bring pads and a spotter, avoid wet rock, and clean your shoes before each try to keep holds in good shape.
wv_county_line_boulders_climbs.parking_note: Drive in through the main gate and continue toward the main overlook. Stop at the first pull-off on your right, the one with picnic tables and a trail marker.
wv_county_line_boulders_climbs.approach: Walk straight down from the picnic area, cross the roadside trail, and follow the rocky path through the trees to the boulders.

wi_burma_road.blurb: A woodland boulder group on the south side of Devil's Lake, reached by user trails rather than any marked path. The boulders are the purple Baraboo quartzite the park is known for: hard, glassy rock with small, subtle holds, where footwork and patience count for more than power. Problems run from easy up to very hard, with a solid base of V0 to V4 and a few real tests above. It is quieter than the busy bluffs. The quartzite dries quickly, and fall is usually the best season; spring tends to bring mud and bugs, and summer can be hot and sticky.

wi_willow_river_state_park.blurb: Steep sport climbing on the walls of the gorge below Willow Falls, in a state park near Hudson. The routes cluster in a big overhanging amphitheater next to the river, on limestone and dolomite, and they favor endurance on large holds. This is a hard-climber's crag: most of the lines fall in the 5.12 and 5.13 range, with only a few easier options. Watch for loose rock and keep people out from underneath you.
wi_willow_river_state_park.parking_note: Take I-94 exit 4 and follow signs into the park. A small lot sits a few hundred yards past the main entrance.
wi_willow_river_state_park.approach: From the lot, follow the trail down a long, gradual slope to the bridge near the falls; the amphitheater is right there beside the river.

wi_reserve_the.blurb: A compact cluster of quartzite boulders high on the South Bluff above Devil's Lake, and one of the better-concentrated spots in the park. A free-standing block with problems on every side anchors the group, and a short cliff band along the rim adds more lines. Grades stretch from V0 well past V10, with a strong middle of V2 to V4 and a good number of hard problems for the experienced. The hike up is steady and takes a while, and the bluff has no official trails, so it feels remote. The slick, fine-edged rock rewards careful footwork.

wy_green_mile_the.blurb: A sport-leaning crag in the Island Area at the west end of Shoshone Canyon, just outside Cody. Most of the routes are bolted, with a modest number of trad lines mixed in, and the bulk of them sit between 5.10 and 5.12, so it works well for climbers already comfortable on steeper, sustained leads. There are a handful of easier and harder outliers at either end. The way in is a trail up to the saddle between the Island and the Arrowhead walls. Expect a canyon setting with road noise below, and check sun and temperature on the day before committing to a long session.
wy_green_mile_the.approach: Hike the trail up to the saddle between the Island wall and the Arrowhead wall; the crag is reached from there.

wy_joint_the.blurb: A steep, tiered cliff high on the Granite side of Sinks Canyon, outside Lander. It is mostly bolted, with only a few trad lines, and the climbing is overhanging and sustained: the great majority of the routes fall between 5.11 and 5.13, with a thin scattering of easier ones. The walk climbs through talus to the base of the cliff, so allow time and watch your footing on loose blocks.
wy_joint_the.parking_note: Continue up Sinks Canyon Road beyond the limestone walls and park at Bruce's Bridge, which also serves the waterfall trail.
